claims.text: The magnitude of the magnetocaloric effect in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys is governed by microstructural inhomogeneities.
Magnetocaloric hysteresis in these alloys is governed by variations in lattice strain, grain-boundary density, and local short-range order.
These microstructural inhomogeneities determine the kinetics of the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Relieving internal strain and increasing local chemical homogeneity can reduce hysteresis while retaining a substantial entropy change.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy forms an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
Rapid deposition produces intrinsic compositional and strain inhomogeneities in the alloy.
Annealing at 350 °C for 4 hours in argon will facilitate microstructural homogenization.
Annealing at 350 °C for 4 hours in argon will relieve internal stress without inducing unwanted phase changes.
The annealing treatment will reduce localized lattice strain and grain-boundary density.
Reduced strain and grain-boundary density will produce a more uniform magnetic-domain structure.
The more uniform microstructure will synchronize the magnetostructural transition and lower its energy barriers.
Lower transition barriers will produce a smoother transition with reduced hysteresis.
Slight grain growth and improved homogeneity may enhance heat exchange by increasing effective surface area.
The as-deposited baseline exhibits a large, sharp, and hysteretic first-order magnetocaloric transition.
The as-deposited baseline has limited heat-exchange performance because of its relatively low surface-to-volume ratio.
Annealed samples will retain a similar or slightly broadened peak magnetic entropy change.
Annealed samples will exhibit substantially narrower magnetic-field cycling hysteresis loops than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will improve reversibility during low-applied-field cooling cycles.
The predictions are expected to hold near room temperature under low applied fields for hexagonal FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys, provided annealing does not induce secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The baseline attributes limited heat exchange to low specimen surface-to-volume ratio, but the mechanism claims that annealing-driven grain growth raises effective surface area and improves heat exchange without specifying any change in specimen geometry. The asserted surface-area rationale is internally inconsistent or insufficiently defined.
